title: Typeform Live-Coding Interview — Audio Prep

chapters.title: How to use this audio
chapters.script:
This is about an hour of preparation for the ninety-minute live coding with George Gillams and Ethan Carlsson on the Typeform AI team, Friday at noon. Two dozen short chapters. Some are the exact words I will say at a specific moment in the interview. Some are pieces of the system I need to know cold, so that when they point at the code I can talk about it without hesitating. Listen all the way through once, then come back to the chapters that matter most: the background pitch, the brief-to-specs flow, and what I say while coding.

Here is the shape of the day. Ninety minutes. A few minutes of introductions, then roughly sixty minutes of coding, then questions at the end. I can use any framework, any database, any editor. They strongly encourage AI tools, and — this is the part that matters — they explicitly assess how I use them. The whole thing is screen-shared, so they follow the code, the prompts I send to the AI, and the overall workflow. Their stated value is simplicity and clarity over completeness or polish.

The task itself has a known shape: they hand me a written brief, I turn it into a small spec, and then I implement it against my scaffold. So the hour is really three movements — understand the brief, write a lean spec, then build, narrating the whole way.

The single most important thing to internalise is this: the narration is the deliverable as much as the code. They grade what comes out of my mouth — the prompts I read aloud, the diffs I review out loud, the trade-offs I name on purpose. Silence is the failure mode. The interview is a conversation, not a recital.

chapters.title: The sixty-second background pitch
chapters.script:
This is what I say when George asks for the sixty-second version of my background, somewhere in the first eight minutes. I say it once, I do not pad it, and I land on the bridge to the role.

Sure. I'm between roles right now. Vitrifi, where I spent four years as a Senior Full Stack, shut down at the start of the year, so I can speak about the architecture concretely. Before that, about twelve years of production web platforms, mostly React, TypeScript, and Go. At Vitrifi we ran five Go services behind a schema-first GraphQL gateway. Around two hundred and forty thousand lines of Go. Close to five thousand commits across four years. Heavy use of an event bus with protocol buffer messages. OpenTelemetry tracing across all of it. The Go work I'd lead with is the stuff I personally designed: custom GraphQL scalars carrying HTML sanitisation through the type system, validation directives enforced by middleware, a couple of small library packages for cross-cutting primitives. Since Vitrifi closed I've been going deep on the AI side. I built an AI engineering roadmap site — around a hundred lessons on agents, evaluations, retrieval-augmented generation, LangGraph, observability. Built it in Next.js and Radix. That's actually what made this role catch my eye. Your stack, my interest area, and I want to ship AI systems daily instead of writing about them.

If I run long, I drop the Go portfolio sentence and let it surface later when George asks what I actually wrote. If I blank completely, the fallback is one sentence: between roles since January when Vitrifi shut down, four years of Go and React on a multi-tenant United Kingdom telecoms platform, now deep on an AI engineering roadmap site and looking to ship daily.

The beats to land: between roles, said calmly once with the reason, then move on. One scale number, not a stat dump. The work I personally designed, which pivots from what we built to what I built. And the bridge: their stack, my interest, ship daily.

chapters.title: Scaffold opener and light spec
chapters.script:
This is minute eight to thirteen of the call. George has said, want to walk us through what you've got, and I have the editor open on the small Go scaffold I brought. Two pieces: a thirty-second opener that hands them the choice, and a short verbal spec before I touch a line of code.

I lead with the opener. I have a small Go scaffold here with a single chat endpoint and three mock Typeform tools — create form, list forms, get responses — so we don't burn time on boilerplate. It streams over server-sent events, the one-direction streaming protocol over plain HTTP. It keeps in-memory session memory, and there's a Next.js frontend wired up if we want it. Happy to extend it, swap a tool out, or start fresh. What would be most useful for you to see? That is the opener. I do not narrate the architecture before they tell me what they want. The point is to hand them the choice, not to deliver a presentation.

Once George names a direction, I do the light spec out loud before opening any new file. The recruiter's warning was sharp on this: a light spec is useful as structure, but it is never the main event. The spec is the muscle, not the show. So this is forty seconds, not fifteen minutes. The single biggest failure mode in this interview is spending fifteen minutes designing the perfect spec and never getting to working code. That is the failure mode I am explicitly defending against.

The script is four sentences. Goal: add a tool the agent can call to compute summary statistics over a form's responses. User: a Typeform customer who wants quick insight without writing structured query language. Success: end-to-end — the user asks, the agent picks the new tool, runs over the store, streams a natural-language summary. Out of scope today: the real Typeform interface, retries, multi-form joins. Then I confirm: does that match what you're looking for?

That's the whole spec. Maybe forty seconds spoken. I might type those four lines into a small file in the project root, another twenty seconds, then close it and start coding. I do not open any methodology directory. I do not whiteboard architecture. If I am still typing the spec at minute thirteen, I stop and start coding immediately. The reason I do the spec at all is that it gives me an anchor: when George asks at minute twenty-three why I did something, I point at the spec and say in scope, here's why, or out of scope, I'd come back to it. The out-of-scope line is the most useful sentence in the whole spec, and I will use it deliberately at least twice while coding.

chapters.title: From brief to working code
chapters.script:
This chapter is the actual task, because it's likely they don't just say "add analytics" — they hand me a written brief and ask me to turn it into a spec, then build it. So here is exactly how I run that, and the timing discipline that makes or breaks it.

First, I ingest the brief. I read it, and before I write anything, I play it back: here's what I think it's asking for — the core requirements, the inputs and outputs, the constraints — and here's what's ambiguous. I do that out loud, and I have the AI tool summarise it too. Reading the brief back is not stalling; it's the thing that stops me from confidently building the wrong feature.

Second, I clarify with the interviewer. The brief will be ambiguous on purpose. I turn the ambiguities into two scope questions for them — is this in scope, or should I assume that. Clarifying scope with the stakeholder before committing is the senior move, and it's exactly the discipline a good spec process forces. The interviewer is the stakeholder here.

Third, I write one lean feature spec. One directory: a requirements file for scope and decisions, a plan file as a short numbered task list, and a validation file for how we know it's done. I keep it to about ten to fifteen minutes. I do not regenerate the mission or the tech-stack documents — those already exist. I do not stand up a heavyweight methodology directory. If I'm still writing specs at minute twenty-five, I have over-processed, and I stop and build.

Then the spec becomes the contract for the rest of the hour. When I skip something, I point at the out-of-scope line. When I add something, I say it's not in what I wrote down, but the model needs it, so I'm adding it. The spec is required here — they asked for it — so I do it crisply and move to code. Specs are the muscle, not the show, even when the spec is the assignment.

Two things make this phase succeed or fail. The first is time. I'm genuinely watching the clock, because the gravitational pull is to keep refining — another requirement, another edge case, a cleaner plan — and every minute there is a minute not spent on the working code they actually want to see. So I give myself a hard stop: if the spec isn't done in about fifteen minutes, whatever I have is the spec, and I start building. The second is who the spec is for. It's for them, as a contract I can point at — in scope, out of scope, here's why. And it's for me, as the thing that keeps me from wandering for the next forty-five minutes. It is not for a methodology. The moment it starts to feel like I'm performing a process rather than framing a problem, I've crossed into the failure mode, and I pull back. A good spec here is three short files a smart person could read in two minutes and know exactly what I'm about to build, and what I'm deliberately not.

chapters.title: What I'll say while coding
chapters.script:
This is the long stretch, minute thirteen to about minute sixty. I'm in the editor, AI assistance running, narrating continuously. The narration is the deliverable as much as the code. The brief said talk through your thinking throughout, and we assess your use of AI tools. Both are graded by what comes out of my mouth, not by what I type.

So I narrate every meaningful action. Before I send a prompt to the AI, I read the prompt out loud. After it generates code, I read the generated code out loud before I accept it, and I say what I'm checking for — that the types match, that the error handling is what I'd write, that nothing has been silently invented. If I disagree with a suggestion, I say so and explain why I'm overriding it. Silent acceptance is the failure mode. If they wanted silent acceptance, they wouldn't be assessing how I use AI tools. They want judgment, not stenography.

I narrate trade-offs deliberately, at least twice. The first comes early, around minute twenty: I'm using an in-memory session store, which is fine for the demo; in production I'd put it behind an interface and back it with Redis or a document store so sessions survive a restart — a one-hour swap, not a redesign. The second lands around minute forty: I'm not adding retries on the language-model call; happy path is fine for showing the loop; in production I'd add exponential backoff and a circuit breaker, and the more interesting question is what idempotency looks like for tools that have side effects, which is where saga compensation comes in. Both lines come out naturally because I've rehearsed them. They're not apologies, they're flags I'm planting on purpose.

I test as I go. After each meaningful change I call the endpoint and narrate what I'm checking. I'm confirming the agent picks the new tool. I'm checking that the tool-result event fires before the streamed text. This is the showstopper for session memory — the model has to remember from turn one that the net-promoter-score form is form one. Testing is part of the workflow they're grading, so I do it on screen rather than switching away.

And if I hit a wall — the AI generates something wrong, a test fails, the endpoint hangs — I narrate the wall, name two ways out, pick one, move on. I do not go silent. Silence at minute thirty-five is worse than picking the wrong fix at minute thirty-five.

It's worth being explicit about what good AI use looks like, because that's the thing under the microscope, and it is not the same as fast AI use. The use they grade up is scoped, reviewed, and attributed. Scoped: I ask for one change at a time, so the diff is small enough to actually read. Reviewed: I read the generated code out loud and say what I'm checking — that the types line up, that the error handling is what I'd write, that it hasn't invented an import or a helper that doesn't exist. Attributed: when I keep a suggestion, I say why it's right; when I override one, I say why it's wrong. The use they grade down is the opposite — a giant prompt, a wall of generated code, and silent acceptance, taking a diff I clearly never read. If they wanted that, they wouldn't be assessing AI use at all; they'd just read the final code. So the signal I want to give, over and over, is judgment: the model drafts, I decide. I'll even narrate a moment where I turn down something that looks fine — this compiles and it's tempting, but it's broader than I asked for and it touches a file I didn't want changed, so I'm rejecting it and re-scoping the prompt. Turning down working code because it's out of scope says more about how I work than any feature I could ship.

chapters.title: Keeping the AI tool consistent
chapters.script:
This runs throughout the coding stretch, and it's worth its own chapter because it's exactly what they said they assess — my use of AI tools. I don't drive the tool from a blank slate every prompt. I keep a small set of scoped instructions — skills — that load the house conventions for this codebase, so the generated code already follows them instead of me re-explaining the style every time.

Three of them matter for this scaffold. One carries the backend conventions: how the tool-definitions slice is shaped, how the dispatch function is structured, how the session store sits behind an interface, how the server-sent-events stream is written. One carries the test conventions: standard-library testing, fake the upstream model with a test server, reset shared state between tests. One carries the tracing conventions: the span names and attributes so a trace is readable later. So when I ask the tool to add a capability, it already writes the tool definition in our shape, writes the test the way the rest of the suite is written, and traces the call like every other tool — without me hand-holding each prompt.

If George asks why bother, the answer is the principle I keep coming back to: make the machine carry the invariant instead of trusting myself to remember it under pressure. A skill stops the tool from free-styling its own conventions, and it's reviewable and version-controlled, so the conventions live next to the code rather than in my head. Same instinct as schema-first contracts and the eval suite — move correctness somewhere that fails earlier than production.

And the honest limit, which I'll say out loud: a skill biases the tool strongly toward the house style, it doesn't guarantee it. That's why I still read every diff out loud before I accept it. The skill narrows what the model is likely to do; the read-aloud review proves what it actually did.

chapters.title: The prompts I'll actually type
chapters.script:
This chapter is the mechanics of the prompts themselves, because how I prompt is the thing on camera. The rule for every prompt is the same: one change at a time, scoped, so each diff is small enough to read out loud. I read the prompt before I send it and the diff before I accept it. I reject anything broader than I asked. The model drafts; I review.

When I add a tool, I do it in two prompts, not one. The first is schema only: add a new entry to the tool-definitions slice, following the exact shape of the existing get-responses tool and our backend conventions, with a description that tells the model when to pick it, and only edit that slice. Saying "follow the shape of the existing tool, per our conventions" is what loads the backend skill, so the output is already in the house style. The second prompt is the implementation: add the matching case to the dispatch function, reusing the same argument parsing and store access as the neighbouring tool, returning a small statistics struct as JSON, about ten to fifteen lines, and don't touch the other cases.

Then I restart and call the endpoint, and I'm checking one thing in particular: that the model routes to the new tool and not the old one. If it picks the wrong tool, I don't reach for the system prompt. I tighten the two tool descriptions so they're mutually exclusive — one returns the raw list, the other computes aggregate statistics — because tool selection is driven by those descriptions, and that's where the model reads intent. If they ask for tests, the prompt is: add a table-driven test following our test conventions and the existing tests — which loads the testing skill.

The one thing I will not do live is run the heavyweight spec-and-roadmap prompts — the ones that create whole methodology directories. Those are planning, off-screen, not the live hour. Live, it's scoped single-change prompts, reviewed out loud.

chapters.title: Walking the main file
chapters.script:
This is the file they're most likely to point at, so I need to narrate it without hesitating. It's the spine of the service, and it's worth knowing every function in it cold.

It starts with the chat handler. That's the entry point — the chat endpoint. It decodes the request — a session id, an optional user id, and the user's message — validates them, and sets the server-sent-events headers so it can stream the reply back token by token. Token by token means the model doesn't return a finished answer in one shot; it generates small fragments, left to right, and we forward each one to the user the instant it arrives. The handler opens a trace span — a span is one timed unit of work, and a trace is the tree of spans for one request; every layer here opens one, so for any conversation I can replay exactly what the agent did and where the time went, all exported to Langfuse over Open Telemetry. The handler appends the user's message to the session history, runs the loop, and at the end emits two events: a meta event carrying the trace ids so the front end can attach thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback, and a done event. Scoring runs in a background goroutine, off the request path, so it adds no latency.

The heart of the file is the run loop, and this is the agent. There's no agent class anywhere; the agent is this loop plus three things — the model, which decides which tool to call; the tool definitions, which are what it's allowed to do; and the conversation history, which is the context it acts on. The loop runs up to five turns: load the history, call the model, and if the model asks for a tool, run it, stream a tool-result event back, append the result, and go round again. It stops when the model answers with no tool call. That loop is what makes this an agent rather than a single model call.

Underneath, stream one is a single streaming model call. It prepends the system prompt, tries the providers in order — the primary first, then a fallback — and for each fragment of text it flushes a frame immediately, which is what pushes the token to the browser instead of buffering to the end. The failover lives there, before any token is flushed, so a provider failure can fall through cleanly. And finally, main wires it all together: it loads config, opens the session store, starts tracing and scoring, picks the tool backend — live Typeform if a token is set, otherwise the in-memory mock — registers the routes, and shuts down gracefully on an interrupt. The shape to remember: a request comes in at the chat handler, the run loop drives the model and the tools, stream one does each model call with failover, and everything streams back over server-sent events.

chapters.title: The live Typeform decision
chapters.script:
This chapter is a decision I made deliberately, and it's a good one to talk about because it shows judgment about risk. The three tools can run two ways: against an in-memory mock, or against the live Typeform interface. They sit behind one interface, and which one is active is chosen at startup by whether a token is set.

For the demo itself, the mock is the right default. It's deterministic, it can't fail on the network mid-call, and it keeps the hour focused on the agent loop rather than on authentication and pagination. That matches their stated value: simplicity over completeness. But I built the live path anyway, behind the same interface, because the interesting engineering is the seam. The line I'll say is: it's behind an interface, so flipping a token turns the same tools into real Typeform calls — the swap is configuration, not a rewrite. And if the live path is ever flaky on the day, unsetting the token reverts instantly to the deterministic mock. The mock is the safety net.

Two things I'll volunteer about the live path, because naming them is the senior move. First, privacy: real responses contain real people's answers — names, emails, free text — and those would flow into the model's context. So I redact email addresses and aggregate rather than dumping raw answers, and I'd never send raw customer responses to a third-party model in production without that. Second, the account I'd demo against is a throwaway with no real responses, so there's no real personal data at stake and the privacy concern is a talking point rather than a live risk. The honest framing is: I know where the data goes, and I designed the seam so the demo stays simple while the real path stays one token away.

chapters.title: Answers to design probes
chapters.script:
This is the band where George or Ethan pushes back. Why did you go with that? Could that prompt go wrong? How would you know this is working in production? These are not gotchas; they're the questions they came in planning to ask.

On why a particular tool name or shape: for an agent the spec is the contract — name, arguments, return type, side effects. I name tools so the model can pick them from intent rather than from copy-pasted examples. A tool called create-form alongside one called analyze-responses gives the model enough signal to route correctly without me hand-tuning the prompt for every phrasing. Same instinct as schema-first GraphQL, with the language model as the new consumer of the contract.

On how I know it's working in production: this is the one Ethan really cares about, so I land it cleanly. Three layers, and the scaffold already has the spine. One: structured telemetry per tool call — a span with tool name, arguments, latency, error code, and model, already exported to Langfuse over Open Telemetry. Two: two behaviour metrics, not uptime — tool-selection accuracy graded by the eval harness, and a turns-to-completion distribution; if accuracy drops or turns creep up after I add a tool, that's the agent regressing, and a health check would never catch it. Three: scoring and sampling — guardrail checks, an optional model-as-judge, and thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback wired to the generation, with about one percent of full conversations sampled so I can read what actually happened. The metric tells me there's a problem; the sample tells me what kind.

And on a question I expect about evals: how do you measure accuracy on something generative, like a summary? I push back on my own number. The bar isn't on whether the prose is good; it's on the parts that have ground truth — did the agent pick the right tool, extract the right field, classify intent. For the generated text I use weaker signals: deterministic checks, a faithfulness rule where any claim must trace to retrieved data, and a model-as-judge validated against a small human-labelled set. The real ground truth is downstream behaviour, which is slow, so offline checks gate deploys. I wouldn't claim a hard accuracy number on pure quality — that would be fake precision. I gate what's measurable and stay honest about what isn't.

chapters.title: What I'd improve next
chapters.script:
This is the exit question the recruiter flagged, probably around minute sixty to seventy-five. Three items, ranked, delivered without looking at notes.

First, surface the observability I already emit. The tracing and the scores are wired; what I'd add is turning the two key metrics — tool-selection accuracy and turns-to-completion — into dashboards and alerts, so a regression pages someone instead of waiting for me to notice. This goes first because without it the next two improvements are guesses. I can't tell whether a new tool made the agent better or worse, or whether a system-prompt change improved refusal quality.

Second, eval coverage on entity resolution. The phrase "the net-promoter-score one" works in my demo because session memory carries form one from the first turn. That's brittle — it works because the model held the context, not because the system guaranteed it. I already have a Go eval harness in the repo, so I'd grow it into maybe twenty scripted conversations covering realistic phrasings, graded on tool-selection accuracy and argument-resolution accuracy. Eval failure breaks the build the same way a fuzz crash does.

Third, event-driven decoupling for long-running tools. The current loop is synchronous; the next request waits for the tool to finish. That's fine for create-form, which is fast, but not for a response export over millions of rows. For those I'd publish a tool-requested event, have a worker consume it, and stream progress and result events back. At Vitrifi we ran this over a messaging bus with protocol buffer events, and the consumer side never got called inline. Same shape, different domain. Plus idempotency keys on create-form, timeouts on every external call, and a dead-letter queue so failures surface instead of disappearing.

Those are the three. Observability first because without it I'm guessing. Evals second because they freeze the behaviour I have. Event-driven third because it unlocks the long-running tools you can't do well synchronously. If George asks which I'd start tomorrow, the answer is observability — that's where the leverage compounds fastest.

chapters.title: Curveball answers
chapters.script:
These are short answers I want at the front of my mind. They could land anywhere.

If asked how a non-technical user would know what the agent can do: discoverability is a user-experience problem, not a code problem. The front end already shows example prompts in the empty state. I'd extend that with suggestion chips driven by the tool registry, so when a tool is added the examples update automatically. Long term, a model-generated capabilities summary. Tooling tells the engineers what's possible; the interface has to tell the user.

If asked why server-sent events instead of WebSockets: one-direction server push fits the token-streaming pattern, plain HTTP works through proxies and load balancers, and the streaming hook on the front end consumes it natively. WebSockets would be over-engineered — I'd reach for them only if the client had to push back mid-stream.

If asked why Go: it matches your stack, the chat loop is mostly orchestration and input-output, the standard library handles HTTP and streaming without a framework, and the team already runs it. No benefit to introducing a second language for this surface.

If asked about tuning the system prompt: I treat it as code. It lives in version control, every change has a commit message explaining what behaviour it shifts, and I run the eval suite against each version. The eval is the test for the prompt.

If asked about multi-user concurrency: sessions are keyed by session id, not user id, so two users hit two sessions naturally. The interesting question is shared state on the form itself, and for that I'd lean on optimistic locking at the interface boundary — the same way we handled concurrent order edits at Vitrifi.

If asked what happens when the user asks for something the agent cannot do: the execute-tool function does strict tool-name validation and returns an unknown-tool error. The model receives that on the next turn and surfaces it to the user. For production I'd add an explicit refusal path in the system prompt, and an evaluation that scores refusal quality, because a confident refusal is a feature and a flailing one is a bug. The model should know what it can do and admit what it can't.

If asked how I'd test it end-to-end: three layers. Unit tests per tool, easy because they're pure functions. A contract test on the server-sent-events format — I have one already. And an eval suite of scripted conversations against the real model, graded on tool-selection accuracy. The eval is the part most agent codebases skip, and a quarter later they regret it because behaviour drifts silently.

If asked what the eval rubric looks like: each scripted conversation has an expected outcome — which tool, which arguments, whether the model declines. I grade per-turn on tool-selection accuracy and argument-resolution accuracy, and per-conversation on whether the user's goal was achieved. The aggregate over the suite is what I track over time, so I can see drift the moment it starts.

If asked about handling an off-topic request mid-conversation: the same path. The model has the tool registry, it routes by intent, and when nothing matches it should say so plainly rather than force a tool that doesn't fit. That's a refusal-quality question, and it's exactly the kind of thing the eval suite is there to pin down.

chapters.title: The title-versus-work question
chapters.script:
If Ethan probes the gap between my title and what they're hiring for — Senior Full Stack versus Go Engineer — this is the answer. Honest, short, with a pivot.

My title at Vitrifi was Senior Full Stack, and across roughly five thousand commits I touched both sides. But the work I'd want to lead with is Go. A package carrying HTML sanitisation through the type system. A composable validation builder. Preload helpers eliminating the N-plus-one problem on list endpoints. A path-traversal fix that resolved to an absolute path, joined the target, and rejected the result if it didn't still prefix the base. Moving address sorting out of the browser into a typed query layer. The frontend work is real too — schema-validated forms with errors routed back to exact fields, a campaign to remove untyped escape hatches. But the design judgement I'm proudest of lives on the Go side, and I'd be glad to go heavier-Go in the next role.

I do not pretend to be a pure Go engineer, and I do not minimise the frontend work. I name the split honestly, point at the Go pieces I designed, and signal direction. Anything else reads as insecure or evasive.

chapters.title: The questions I'll ask
chapters.script:
Last five minutes. They'll ask if I have questions. Two is the sweet spot. I pick the right one for the right person.

For Ethan, the technical one. I noticed event-driven programming is something the team leans on. At Vitrifi we ran a messaging bus with protocol buffer events and signature verification on consume, so the consumer side picked up state transitions rather than being called inline. I'm curious how the agent loop is shaped here — more event-driven internally, with workers picking up tool-requested events and streaming results back, or a synchronous tool loop with streaming on the edge. The answer changes how I'd extend it for longer-running tools.

For George, the broader one. You're a frontend lead hiring a Go engineer. How does the team think about the boundary between the agent's behaviour and the user-experience layer — where does prompt engineering live, and where does product design take over? That boundary is one of the harder problems in agent-driven products, and I'm curious how you draw it.

If both feel like too much, the backup is: what's the hardest problem the team hasn't cracked yet. Safe, opens any direction.

And the discipline — the things I will not say. I will not name the spec-driven methodology as a brand; light is the point, not the label. I will not open a methodology scratch directory on screen, or whiteboard a diagram. I will not reference anything personal about George or Ethan from their profiles. I will not pre-build an extra tool just in case, because the moment they ask for something different I'll be tempted to force-fit, and the force-fit shows. And I will not sit silent while the AI generates code — I read every line out loud before I accept it, because that is the behaviour they're assessing, not just the code.

That's the core flow of the ninety minutes, start to finish. The chapters that follow go deeper on the things they're most likely to probe — the Go work I personally did at Vitrifi, the architecture and the anchor stories behind it, the eval harness, how I want to carry myself in the room, and the honest reason I want this role.

chapters.title: What I wrote in Go
chapters.script:
When George or Ethan asks what I actually wrote — not what the team built, what I designed — this is the chapter. It's first person and specific, because vague claims are worthless and specific ones are checkable.

The piece I'd lead with is a package I created called x-h-t-m-l. The problem was concrete: notification bodies and activity messages needed to carry limited formatting, which means user-influenced markup was going to be stored and later rendered in another user's browser — the exact setup for cross-site scripting. My solution was a custom GraphQL scalar with its own marshal and unmarshal functions, so the type system itself carried the safety guarantee rather than leaving it to whoever wrote the resolver. On unmarshal, the value ran through an HTML sanitiser with a deliberately small allow-list of style properties, and a stricter links-only variant for notifications where the only thing that should survive is a controlled anchor. It's a clean example of moving a security property from something a developer must remember into something the type system enforces by default.

The second package was x-validate, a composable validation builder for subscribers and service orders. A flat list of required fields wasn't enough, because correctness depended on context, and getting it wrong had direct commercial cost — too strict and a legitimate order was blocked, too loose and a broken order failed later inside a carrier interaction. The builder let the rule set be assembled per context. I made a specific change where I relaxed historical rules that were too strict, deleted the test cases that pinned the wrong behaviour, and kept the genuine business constraint, which was a whitelisted email domain. Deleting tests is normally a smell, and here it was the correct move precisely because the tests encoded a requirement we'd decided was wrong.

The third package was x-g-q-l, preload helpers for eliminating the N-plus-one problem on list queries. List endpoints had the classic issue: one query for the list, then one more query per row for a related entity, so a page of fifty rows became fifty-one round trips. The package let a resolver declare which related entities it needed, so they were fetched in a bounded number of queries instead of one per row.

Then two security fixes I can describe down to the mechanism. The first was a path-traversal vulnerability in a document-generation tool. My fix resolved the output directory to an absolute path, joined the target filename onto that absolute base, and then explicitly rejected the operation if the resulting path didn't still begin with the resolved base — so an escape was caught before any file handle opened. I also pinned the output filename to a constant, removing filename injection as a separate vector. The second was file permissions: I introduced a single shared constant set to owner-only read and write, and applied it at the write sites that had been permissive. The detail that makes it a real fix rather than a one-off patch is that it was one shared constant, so the secure default became importable and consistent rather than re-decided at each call site.

The last piece is a performance change with a satisfying shape: moving address sorting out of the browser and into the database. The original design fetched addresses and sorted them on the frontend, which was slow and, worse, sorted them lexically — so building number two sorted after building number ten, which is wrong to a human reading an address list. I threaded sort and order parameters down into the query, and the natural numeric ordering happened in the database using a regular-expression match to extract the leading number. I deleted the now-dead frontend sort utility in the same change, because a fix that leaves the superseded code in place is only half a fix.

The throughline across all of it is one instinct: move correctness earlier. From runtime to compile time through generated types. From scattered checks to declarative directives enforced by middleware. That single principle is the engineering judgement I'd bring here — and it's the same reason I care about evals for agents.

chapters.title: Architecture and anchor stories
chapters.script:
This is the context behind those packages, and the set of stories I reach for when a trade-off question opens up. I don't recite the architecture; I keep these ready and pull the one that fits the question.

The platform was multi-tenant, for the United Kingdom wholesale broadband market. We ran five Go services behind a schema-first GraphQL gateway. Inter-service flow went over an event bus with protocol buffer messages. Long-running, stateful orders ran on a workflow engine so they could survive restarts and retries. And OpenTelemetry tracing was threaded across all of it — HTTP, the service-to-service calls, and the event-bus subjects — so a single request could be followed end to end.

The first anchor story is observability, and I've already covered its shape: structured signal per operation, a couple of metrics that describe behaviour rather than uptime, and sampling so I can read what actually happened. The point of the story is that I've done this for real across a distributed system, not just for a single service.

The second is event-driven decoupling. State transitions were published as protocol buffer events, and the consumer side — what we called the activator — picked them up rather than being called inline by the portal. There was signature verification on consume, so a consumer could trust the message. The detail I'm proudest of is that tenant information was modelled as a field on the proto message, so audit and isolation travelled identically through a synchronous request and through an asynchronous event — never two divergent code paths. That's the story I tell when they ask about extending the agent to long-running tools.

The third is multi-tenant isolation and secure-by-default directives. Validation directives ran in middleware before any resolver, so a new resolver was secure by default rather than secure if you remembered. That's the same instinct as the x-h-t-m-l scalar: make the safe thing the automatic thing. When they ask how I think about safety in an agent — refusals, tool permissions, what the model is allowed to touch — this is the lineage I draw on.

The reason I keep these as stories rather than facts is that an interviewer doesn't want a tour of an architecture. They want to see judgement applied to a concrete problem. So I wait for the question, then I reach for the one story that answers it, and I land it in under a minute.

chapters.title: The eval harness, in depth
chapters.script:
Evals are the part of agent engineering I most want to talk about, because it's the part most teams skip, and it's the clearest bridge from my Vitrifi instinct — move correctness earlier — to this domain.

Here's the framing I use. A traditional test asserts a function returns the right value. An eval asserts a non-deterministic system behaves the right way often enough. For an agent, the two things worth grading are tool-selection accuracy — did the model pick the right tool for the request — and argument-resolution accuracy — did it fill in the right arguments, including resolving references like "the net-promoter-score one" to the correct form. Each scripted conversation has an expected outcome: which tool, which arguments, or whether the model should decline. I grade per turn on those two axes, and per conversation on whether the user's goal was actually achieved.

Why this matters so much: as I add tools, the descriptions start to overlap, and the model can begin routing badly in ways no unit test would catch, because the unit tests still pass — the tool itself works, the model just stopped picking it. Without an eval suite I can't tell whether a change made the agent better or worse. With one, an eval failure breaks the build exactly the way a fuzz crash does. That turns "the agent feels worse lately" into a red line in continuous integration.

In the scaffold the eval harness is already there, and it's deliberately all-Go with no second language in the test path — a Go provider drives the live chat server, grades the tool selection, and a codeless assertion reads the result. The reason I built it that way is the same reason I keep the rest of the stack lean: fewer moving parts, and the evals live next to the code they grade.

The honest limit, which I'll volunteer: evals on generative quality — is this summary good — are soft. I gate the parts with ground truth hard, and for the prose I use faithfulness checks and a model-as-judge validated against a small human-labelled set. I don't claim a precise accuracy number on quality, because that would be fake precision. I gate what's measurable and stay honest about the rest.

chapters.title: Rehearsal, pacing, and the room
chapters.script:
This chapter isn't content for the interview; it's how I carry myself through it. Worth listening to the morning of.

Start with the first line, because nerves live there. The opening sentence — between roles right now, Vitrifi shut down at the start of the year — I drill until it comes out calm and unbothered. Once that lands, the rest flows. If I'm tense, it's because I'm rushing the open; slow the first sentence down.

Pacing is the thing that decides this interview. There are about sixty minutes of coding, and the failure mode is spending the first twenty-five on a perfect spec and never reaching working code. So the spec is fast — ten to fifteen minutes, one lean feature spec — and then I'm building. If I notice I'm still specifying past minute twenty-five, I stop mid-sentence and start coding. Shipping a small thing that works beats designing a big thing that doesn't.

Narrate continuously. The longest I should be silent is about ten seconds. When the AI is generating, I fill the gap by explaining why I scoped the prompt the way I did. When I hit a wall — a failing test, a hung endpoint, a wrong suggestion — I narrate the wall, name two ways out, pick one, and move. Silence at minute thirty-five is worse than picking the wrong fix at minute thirty-five, because silence reads as stuck and a decision reads as engineering.

Test on screen, not in my head. After each meaningful change I call the endpoint and say what I'm checking. Testing is part of the workflow they grade, so I make it visible.

And the hygiene, done before I join the call: the scratch notes, the methodology directory, and any research files are hidden from the editor's file tree. The specs directory will be on screen, because the spec is the deliverable, but nothing that looks like a script or a cheat sheet is visible. I want them watching me think, not reading my preparation. The other practical check, done the night before, not in the first five minutes: screen recording is enabled for the video-call app in the operating-system privacy settings, and I've run one real test share — because the worst possible start is fumbling permissions while they watch.

chapters.title: Why this role, honestly
chapters.script:
If George asks why this role, or why the AI side, I don't reach for a pitch. I tell the truth, because the truth is good.

Building lead-generation systems and the roadmap site showed me the part I enjoy most isn't the model itself — it's the engineering around it. The evals, the grounding, the routing, the observability. The work that turns a flaky demo into something you can actually trust in production. That's the same work I did at Vitrifi, just with a language model as the new component, and it's what your roadmap as a team is about — more tools, smarter routing, better grounding.

On being between roles: I'm not going to dance around it. Vitrifi shut down, I've used the time since to go deep on exactly this domain, and I'm being selective about where I land rather than taking the first thing. I want to ship these systems daily instead of writing about them. That's the honest motivation, and it happens to line up exactly with what you're hiring for.

I won't oversell the roadmap site. If it comes up, it's evidence of where my attention has been for the last few months, not a credential. And I won't pretend the runway doesn't matter — it's what lets me be selective and relaxed in the room. But that shows in how I carry myself, not in anything I say.

chapters.title: The two lists
chapters.script:
I'll close with the discipline, because the say-list and the don't-say-list are the same list read from two sides, and both have to hold under pressure when the conversation gets warm.

The things I will say, because they're rehearsed. The opening line, once, with the reason, then move on. The short verbal spec before I code. The out-of-scope line at least twice while coding, as a deliberate skip. Two trade-offs out loud: in-memory store fine for the demo, Redis in production; and skipping retries on the model call, happy path first, exponential backoff and a circuit breaker for production. The three-item improvement list when they ask what's next: surface the observability I already emit, eval coverage on entity resolution, event-driven decoupling for long-running tools. And the two questions at the end, directed at the right person.

The things I will not say, and why each stays in the box. I will not name the spec-driven methodology as a brand — light is the point, not the label, and naming it makes it the main event, which is the failure mode I'm avoiding. I will not open a methodology scratch directory or whiteboard a diagram. I will not reference anything personal about George or Ethan from their profiles — the cost of that is far higher than the value. I will not bring up anyone's side projects unprompted; the role is Go, and if another language comes up naturally I mention my own work briefly and move on. I will not pre-build an extra tool just in case, because the moment they ask for something different I'll be tempted to force-fit, and the force-fit shows. And I will not sit silent while the AI generates code; I read every line out loud before I accept it.

Those two lists, read from both sides, are the discipline that holds the whole thing together.

chapters.title: My lead-gen AI story
chapters.script:
When George asks what I've actually built in AI — beyond writing a roadmap site — this is the deep answer, and it's the one that maps most directly onto what their team does.

It's a business-to-business lead-generation system. An agentic pipeline: it discovers companies, enriches them, finds the right contacts, and drafts outreach. The part relevant to this role is the agent layer. There's a set of specialised graphs, and an orchestration step decides which one to run for a given request. That is exactly the problem their product has — which tool, or which capability, does this natural-language request map to. So when I talk about tool selection in the scaffold, I'm talking about a smaller version of something I've already built at scale.

Three things in it I'd call out, because they're the things their roadmap is about. First, it's eval-first. Every prompt change or model change has to clear an accuracy bar before it ships, so behaviour doesn't drift silently as the system grows. Second, grounding. The model's outputs are schema-constrained and validated against a taxonomy, so it can't invent a category that doesn't exist — the model proposes, the schema disposes. Third, multi-model routing. A cheap, fast model handles the easy cases, and the system only escalates to an expensive reasoning model when confidence is low, which keeps cost sane at batch scale.

On the stack, I'm honest about the split: the agent runtime there is Python on LangGraph, the serving layer is TypeScript over a Postgres database, and the hot machine-learning kernels are Rust. There's no Go in that one — which is part of why I built the Go scaffold for today, to show the backend craft in their language specifically.

And if they push on how I measure any of it — the same answer as before. The accuracy bar sits on the parts that have ground truth: did it pick the right contact, extract the right field, classify intent correctly. The generative copy gets faithfulness checks and a model-as-judge validated against human labels. I don't claim a hard number on pure quality, because that's fake precision. The throughline, again: move correctness somewhere it fails earlier than production. Their roadmap is more tools, smarter routing, better grounding — and that's the exact triangle I've already been building in.

chapters.title: When it goes wrong
chapters.script:
Something will break during the hour. The AI will generate wrong code, a test will fail, the endpoint will hang, the model will pick the wrong tool. This chapter is the most important one, because how I handle a wall is more revealing than the happy path, and a calm recovery is one of the strongest signals I can give.

The rule above all others: do not go silent. When I hit a wall, I narrate the wall, name two ways out, pick one, and move. Silence at minute thirty-five reads as stuck; a decision at minute thirty-five reads as engineering, even if it's the wrong decision.

The specific walls and how I take each. If the AI over-reaches and edits a file I didn't ask it to touch, I reject the diff out loud — too broad, let me scope that down — and re-prompt with a tighter instruction. Rejecting on camera is a positive; it shows I'm reading, not rubber-stamping. If the model routes to the wrong tool, I don't hack the system prompt; I tighten the two tool descriptions so they're mutually exclusive, because that's where the model reads intent. If the endpoint hangs or errors, I read the server log out loud and check the obvious thing first rather than guessing. If the live integration is flaky on the network, I say it — and fall back to the deterministic mock by unsetting the token, because that fallback is exactly why the interface exists.

And the wall that matters most under time pressure: running low on the clock. If I'm at minute fifty-five with a half-built feature, I cut scope to the core the spec named, get that working end-to-end, and say out loud what I'd come back to. A small thing that runs beats a big thing that doesn't, and naming the cut is the out-of-scope muscle one more time. The anti-pattern I'm guarding against is rabbit-holing — if I've been stuck on the same error for more than two minutes, I stop, step back, and either simplify or skip. Persistence on the wrong thing is not a virtue here.

That's how I hold steady when it wobbles.

chapters.title: A worked example
chapters.script:
Let me run the whole flow once on a concrete example, so the abstract steps have a shape. Say George hands me a brief that reads, roughly: users want to ask the assistant for a quick read on a form's results — averages, counts, a sense of how people responded — without exporting anything or leaving the chat. That's the brief. Here's the hour from there.

First I ingest it and read it back, out loud. So the ask is a natural-language analytics capability over an existing form's responses — summary numbers and a short narrative read, no export, no new screen necessarily. I'd rather confirm the edges than guess them. That playback alone tells them I don't just start typing at the first prompt.

Then I clarify with two questions, because the brief is deliberately a little open. First: is this numbers only — averages and counts — or also a written summary of the free-text answers, which is a softer, fuzzier thing to get right? Second: is it always whatever form we're already talking about, or should the user be able to name any form they own? Suppose George says numbers plus a short narrative, and any form by name. Now I have a contract, and it took ninety seconds.

Now the spec — about ten minutes, one directory, three short files. The requirements file: a tool the agent can call to compute summary statistics over a named form's responses, returning counts, a per-field distribution, and a numeric average where the field is numeric; the model writes the narrative from those numbers. In scope: numbers and a streamed summary. Out of scope today: real-time updates, export, joining across multiple forms, and the real Typeform interface — the mock store is fine for the hour. One decision recorded: the tool returns structured statistics as data, and the model phrases them, so the what and the how stay separate. The plan file is four numbered task groups: add the tool definition; implement the dispatch case that computes the statistics; confirm the agent routes to it from an analytics-style phrasing; add one test. The validation file is how we'll know it's done: the agent picks the new tool for a phrasing like what's the average score on the net-promoter form, it returns the right counts on a seeded form, it streams a readable summary, an unknown form name comes back as a structured error rather than a crash, and the test passes. That's the whole spec. I read it back in two sentences, confirm it matches, and close the file.

Then I build, narrating. First prompt, schema only: add a tool definition following the shape of the existing get-responses tool and our backend conventions, one required form-identifier argument, a description that says it computes aggregate statistics and is for analytics questions rather than the raw list. I read the prompt aloud, send it, read the diff aloud — one new entry, argument required, nothing else touched — and accept. Second prompt, the implementation: add the matching dispatch case, reuse the same argument parsing and store access as the neighbouring tool, compute a small statistics struct, return it as JSON, about a dozen lines. I read that diff aloud too, checking the error path on a missing identifier and that the struct is what I'd write, and accept. Then I restart and call the endpoint, and I say what I'm watching for: that the model routes to the new tool and not the old one, and that a tool-result event fires before the streamed summary. If it routes wrong, I tighten the two descriptions so they're mutually exclusive and try again — at the descriptions, not the system prompt, because that's where the model reads intent.

By about minute twenty-five to thirty I have a working end-to-end slice: a real question goes in, the agent picks the new tool, runs it over the store, and streams back a summary. From there the time goes into making it solid and narrating trade-offs — the in-memory store is fine for the demo, retries are a production concern, the statistics are computed in Go which is fine for small forms but I'd push aggregation down to storage for millions of rows. And if I'm tight on time near the end, I cut to the core the spec named, get that clean, and say out loud what I'd come back to.

The whole point of walking it this way: in roughly ten or twelve minutes I went from an ambiguous brief to a written contract and a working first slice, and every step of it was visible on the screen and explained out loud. That is the thing they are actually assessing — not whether I can write a statistics function, but how I take a vague request, make it concrete, drive the tool, check my own work, and keep talking the whole way.

chapters.title: Narrowing an abstract brief
chapters.script:
Here's a second worked example, and I'm choosing a deliberately vaguer brief than the last one, because the vaguer it is, the more the clarify-and-cut move earns its keep. Say George says: right now the assistant can create a form, list forms, and pull responses for one; what we'd like is for someone to ask it to make sense of what came back — which responses need attention, who's unhappy — rather than just dumping rows. Take it where you think it should go.

That brief is doing something sneaky, and naming it is the first point I score. It quietly bundles three different features into one sentence. Needs attention could mean sentiment — flag the negative answers. It could mean completeness — surface the responses someone started and abandoned. And who's unhappy could be a simple read on the rating fields, or it could mean running every free-text answer through the model to judge its tone. Those are not one feature. They're three, and they carry very different amounts of risk in a sixty-minute window.

So I do not start typing. I play it back first: the gap here is that today I can fetch raw responses, but nothing helps the user interpret them — so this is an interpretation tool, and let me pin down which interpretation before I write a line.

Then I clarify with two questions, aimed at the interviewer as the stakeholder. First: by needs attention, do you mean sentiment — flagging negative answers — or completeness — partial responses that were never finished? They're different builds, and I'd rather do one of them well than both badly. Second: for the unhappy read, do you want me leaning on the structured rating fields, where there's a clean numeric signal, or actually sending answers to the model to judge tone? And then I propose my own cut, so they see judgement rather than just questions: my instinct for one testable hour is a new analyze-responses tool, sentiment derived from the numeric rating fields, fully deterministic so it unit-tests cleanly — and I'd note model-judged tone and completeness tracking as the obvious next steps. Does that match what you want to see?

Suppose George says yes, keep it deterministic, structured fields are fine. I've just turned a three-feature brief into one buildable slice, justified the cut by the clock, and named exactly what I'm deferring — in about two minutes.

The spec is then the same lean three files. Requirements: a tool that computes a sentiment summary over a named form's responses from its rating fields, returning counts and a simple positive-versus-negative split, with the model phrasing the result. In scope: deterministic sentiment from structured fields, streamed back as a summary. Out of scope today, written down explicitly: model-judged tone on free text, completeness and partial-response tracking, and any follow-up or reminder drafting. The plan is the familiar four task groups — the tool definition, the dispatch case that computes the split, confirm routing, one table-driven test. Validation: the agent routes to the new tool for a phrasing like who's unhappy on the net-promoter form, it returns the right split on a seeded form, an unknown form name comes back as a structured error, and the test passes.

And that's the move I most want to have in my hands on the day. The first example showed the happy path on a fairly clean brief. This one shows the harder, more realistic case: a brief that's vague on purpose, where the whole signal is whether I can hear the three features hiding inside one sentence, pick the one worth building, and say out loud what I'm leaving for later. The cut is the senior move, and the out-of-scope line is where it lives.

That's the whole preparation — the flow of the ninety minutes, the deeper material behind it, and two worked examples to make it concrete. Listen until the cadence is mine, then close the file. The interview is a conversation, not a recital.

full_script:
## How to use this audio

This is about an hour of preparation for the ninety-minute live coding with George Gillams and Ethan Carlsson on the Typeform AI team, Friday at noon. Two dozen short chapters. Some are the exact words I will say at a specific moment in the interview. Some are pieces of the system I need to know cold, so that when they point at the code I can talk about it without hesitating. Listen all the way through once, then come back to the chapters that matter most: the background pitch, the brief-to-specs flow, and what I say while coding.

Here is the shape of the day. Ninety minutes. A few minutes of introductions, then roughly sixty minutes of coding, then questions at the end. I can use any framework, any database, any editor. They strongly encourage AI tools, and — this is the part that matters — they explicitly assess how I use them. The whole thing is screen-shared, so they follow the code, the prompts I send to the AI, and the overall workflow. Their stated value is simplicity and clarity over completeness or polish.

The task itself has a known shape: they hand me a written brief, I turn it into a small spec, and then I implement it against my scaffold. So the hour is really three movements — understand the brief, write a lean spec, then build, narrating the whole way.

The single most important thing to internalise is this: the narration is the deliverable as much as the code. They grade what comes out of my mouth — the prompts I read aloud, the diffs I review out loud, the trade-offs I name on purpose. Silence is the failure mode. The interview is a conversation, not a recital.

## The sixty-second background pitch

This is what I say when George asks for the sixty-second version of my background, somewhere in the first eight minutes. I say it once, I do not pad it, and I land on the bridge to the role.

Sure. I'm between roles right now. Vitrifi, where I spent four years as a Senior Full Stack, shut down at the start of the year, so I can speak about the architecture concretely. Before that, about twelve years of production web platforms, mostly React, TypeScript, and Go. At Vitrifi we ran five Go services behind a schema-first GraphQL gateway. Around two hundred and forty thousand lines of Go. Close to five thousand commits across four years. Heavy use of an event bus with protocol buffer messages. OpenTelemetry tracing across all of it. The Go work I'd lead with is the stuff I personally designed: custom GraphQL scalars carrying HTML sanitisation through the type system, validation directives enforced by middleware, a couple of small library packages for cross-cutting primitives. Since Vitrifi closed I've been going deep on the AI side. I built an AI engineering roadmap site — around a hundred lessons on agents, evaluations, retrieval-augmented generation, LangGraph, observability. Built it in Next.js and Radix. That's actually what made this role catch my eye. Your stack, my interest area, and I want to ship AI systems daily instead of writing about them.

If I run long, I drop the Go portfolio sentence and let it surface later when George asks what I actually wrote. If I blank completely, the fallback is one sentence: between roles since January when Vitrifi shut down, four years of Go and React on a multi-tenant United Kingdom telecoms platform, now deep on an AI engineering roadmap site and looking to ship daily.

The beats to land: between roles, said calmly once with the reason, then move on. One scale number, not a stat dump. The work I personally designed, which pivots from what we built to what I built. And the bridge: their stack, my interest, ship daily.

## Scaffold opener and light spec

This is minute eight to thirteen of the call. George has said, want to walk us through what you've got, and I have the editor open on the small Go scaffold I brought. Two pieces: a thirty-second opener that hands them the choice, and a short verbal spec before I touch a line of code.

I lead with the opener. I have a small Go scaffold here with a single chat endpoint and three mock Typeform tools — create form, list forms, get responses — so we don't burn time on boilerplate. It streams over server-sent events, the one-direction streaming protocol over plain HTTP. It keeps in-memory session memory, and there's a Next.js frontend wired up if we want it. Happy to extend it, swap a tool out, or start fresh. What would be most useful for you to see? That is the opener. I do not narrate the architecture before they tell me what they want. The point is to hand them the choice, not to deliver a presentation.

Once George names a direction, I do the light spec out loud before opening any new file. The recruiter's warning was sharp on this: a light spec is useful as structure, but it is never the main event. The spec is the muscle, not the show. So this is forty seconds, not fifteen minutes. The single biggest failure mode in this interview is spending fifteen minutes designing the perfect spec and never getting to working code. That is the failure mode I am explicitly defending against.

The script is four sentences. Goal: add a tool the agent can call to compute summary statistics over a form's responses. User: a Typeform customer who wants quick insight without writing structured query language. Success: end-to-end — the user asks, the agent picks the new tool, runs over the store, streams a natural-language summary. Out of scope today: the real Typeform interface, retries, multi-form joins. Then I confirm: does that match what you're looking for?

That's the whole spec. Maybe forty seconds spoken. I might type those four lines into a small file in the project root, another twenty seconds, then close it and start coding. I do not open any methodology directory. I do not whiteboard architecture. If I am still typing the spec at minute thirteen, I stop and start coding immediately. The reason I do the spec at all is that it gives me an anchor: when George asks at minute twenty-three why I did something, I point at the spec and say in scope, here's why, or out of scope, I'd come back to it. The out-of-scope line is the most useful sentence in the whole spec, and I will use it deliberately at least twice while coding.

## From brief to working code

This chapter is the actual task, because it's likely they don't just say "add analytics" — they hand me a written brief and ask me to turn it into a spec, then build it. So here is exactly how I run that, and the timing discipline that makes or breaks it.

First, I ingest the brief. I read it, and before I write anything, I play it back: here's what I think it's asking for — the core requirements, the inputs and outputs, the constraints — and here's what's ambiguous. I do that out loud, and I have the AI tool summarise it too. Reading the brief back is not stalling; it's the thing that stops me from confidently building the wrong feature.

Second, I clarify with the interviewer. The brief will be ambiguous on purpose. I turn the ambiguities into two scope questions for them — is this in scope, or should I assume that. Clarifying scope with the stakeholder before committing is the senior move, and it's exactly the discipline a good spec process forces. The interviewer is the stakeholder here.

Third, I write one lean feature spec. One directory: a requirements file for scope and decisions, a plan file as a short numbered task list, and a validation file for how we know it's done. I keep it to about ten to fifteen minutes. I do not regenerate the mission or the tech-stack documents — those already exist. I do not stand up a heavyweight methodology directory. If I'm still writing specs at minute twenty-five, I have over-processed, and I stop and build.

Then the spec becomes the contract for the rest of the hour. When I skip something, I point at the out-of-scope line. When I add something, I say it's not in what I wrote down, but the model needs it, so I'm adding it. The spec is required here — they asked for it — so I do it crisply and move to code. Specs are the muscle, not the show, even when the spec is the assignment.

Two things make this phase succeed or fail. The first is time. I'm genuinely watching the clock, because the gravitational pull is to keep refining — another requirement, another edge case, a cleaner plan — and every minute there is a minute not spent on the working code they actually want to see. So I give myself a hard stop: if the spec isn't done in about fifteen minutes, whatever I have is the spec, and I start building. The second is who the spec is for. It's for them, as a contract I can point at — in scope, out of scope, here's why. And it's for me, as the thing that keeps me from wandering for the next forty-five minutes. It is not for a methodology. The moment it starts to feel like I'm performing a process rather than framing a problem, I've crossed into the failure mode, and I pull back. A good spec here is three short files a smart person could read in two minutes and know exactly what I'm about to build, and what I'm deliberately not.

## What I'll say while coding

This is the long stretch, minute thirteen to about minute sixty. I'm in the editor, AI assistance running, narrating continuously. The narration is the deliverable as much as the code. The brief said talk through your thinking throughout, and we assess your use of AI tools. Both are graded by what comes out of my mouth, not by what I type.

So I narrate every meaningful action. Before I send a prompt to the AI, I read the prompt out loud. After it generates code, I read the generated code out loud before I accept it, and I say what I'm checking for — that the types match, that the error handling is what I'd write, that nothing has been silently invented. If I disagree with a suggestion, I say so and explain why I'm overriding it. Silent acceptance is the failure mode. If they wanted silent acceptance, they wouldn't be assessing how I use AI tools. ## Keeping the AI tool consistent

This runs throughout the coding stretch, and it's worth its own chapter because it's exactly what they said they assess — my use of AI tools. I don't drive the tool from a blank slate every prompt. I keep a small set of scoped instructions — skills — that load the house conventions for this codebase, so the generated code already follows them instead of me re-explaining the style every time.

Three of them matter for this scaffold. One carries the backend conventions: how the tool-definitions slice is shaped, how the dispatch function is structured, how the session store sits behind an interface, how the server-sent-events stream is written. One carries the test conventions: standard-library testing, fake the upstream model with a test server, reset shared state between tests. One carries the tracing conventions: the span names and attributes so a trace is readable later. So when I ask the tool to add a capability, it already writes the tool definition in our shape, writes the test the way the rest of the suite is written, and traces the call like every other tool — without me hand-holding each prompt.

If George asks why bother, the answer is the principle I keep coming back to: make the machine carry the invariant instead of trusting myself to remember it under pressure. A skill stops the tool from free-styling its own conventions, and it's reviewable and version-controlled, so the conventions live next to the code rather than in my head. Same instinct as schema-first contracts and the eval suite — move correctness somewhere that fails earlier than production.

And the honest limit, which I'll say out loud: a skill biases the tool strongly toward the house style, it doesn't guarantee it. That's why I still read every diff out loud before I accept it. The skill narrows what the model is likely to do; the read-aloud review proves what it actually did.

## The prompts I'll actually type

This chapter is the mechanics of the prompts themselves, because how I prompt is the thing on camera. The rule for every prompt is the same: one change at a time, scoped, so each diff is small enough to read out loud. I read the prompt before I send it and the diff before I accept it. When I add a tool, I do it in two prompts, not one. The first is schema only: add a new entry to the tool-definitions slice, following the exact shape of the existing get-responses tool and our backend conventions, with a description that tells the model when to pick it, and only edit that slice. Saying "follow the shape of the existing tool, per our conventions" is what loads the backend skill, so the output is already in the house style. The second prompt is the implementation: add the matching case to the dispatch function, reusing the same argument parsing and store access as the neighbouring tool, returning a small statistics struct as JSON, about ten to fifteen lines, and don't touch the other cases.

Then I restart and call the endpoint, and I'm checking one thing in particular: that the model routes to the new tool and not the old one. If it picks the wrong tool, I don't reach for the system prompt. I tighten the two tool descriptions so they're mutually exclusive — one returns the raw list, the other computes aggregate statistics — because tool selection is driven by those descriptions, and that's where the model reads intent. If they ask for tests, the prompt is: add a table-driven test following our test conventions and the existing tests — which loads the testing skill.

The one thing I will not do live is run the heavyweight spec-and-roadmap prompts — the ones that create whole methodology directories. Those are planning, off-screen, not the live hour. Live, it's scoped single-change prompts, reviewed out loud.

## Walking the main file

This is the file they're most likely to point at, so I need to narrate it without hesitating. It's the spine of the service, and it's worth knowing every function in it cold.

It starts with the chat handler. That's the entry point — the chat endpoint. It decodes the request — a session id, an optional user id, and the user's message — validates them, and sets the server-sent-events headers so it can stream the reply back token by token. Token by token means the model doesn't return a finished answer in one shot; it generates small fragments, left to right, and we forward each one to the user the instant it arrives. The handler opens a trace span — a span is one timed unit of work, and a trace is the tree of spans for one request; every layer here opens one, so for any conversation I can replay exactly what the agent did and where the time went, all exported to Langfuse over Open Telemetry. The handler appends the user's message to the session history, runs the loop, and at the end emits two events: a meta event carrying the trace ids so the front end can attach thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback, and a done event. Scoring runs in a background goroutine, off the request path, so it adds no latency.

The heart of the file is the run loop, and this is the agent. There's no agent class anywhere; the agent is this loop plus three things — the model, which decides which tool to call; the tool definitions, which are what it's allowed to do; and the conversation history, which is the context it acts on. The loop runs up to five turns: load the history, call the model, and if the model asks for a tool, run it, stream a tool-result event back, append the result, and go round again. It stops when the model answers with no tool call. That loop is what makes this an agent rather than a single model call.

Underneath, stream one is a single streaming model call. It prepends the system prompt, tries the providers in order — the primary first, then a fallback — and for each fragment of text it flushes a frame immediately, which is what pushes the token to the browser instead of buffering to the end. The failover lives there, before any token is flushed, so a provider failure can fall through cleanly. And finally, main wires it all together: it loads config, opens the session store, starts tracing and scoring, picks the tool backend — live Typeform if a token is set, otherwise the in-memory mock — registers the routes, and shuts down gracefully on an interrupt. The shape to remember: a request comes in at the chat handler, the run loop drives the model and the tools, stream one does each model call with failover, and everything streams back over server-sent events.

## The live Typeform decision

This chapter is a decision I made deliberately, and it's a good one to talk about because it shows judgment about risk. The three tools can run two ways: against an in-memory mock, or against the live Typeform interface. They sit behind one interface, and which one is active is chosen at startup by whether a token is set.

For the demo itself, the mock is the right default. It's deterministic, it can't fail on the network mid-call, and it keeps the hour focused on the agent loop rather than on authentication and pagination. That matches their stated value: simplicity over completeness. But I built the live path anyway, behind the same interface, because the interesting engineering is the seam. The line I'll say is: it's behind an interface, so flipping a token turns the same tools into real Typeform calls — the swap is configuration, not a rewrite. And if the live path is ever flaky on the day, unsetting the token reverts instantly to the deterministic mock. The mock is the safety net.

Two things I'll volunteer about the live path, because naming them is the senior move. First, privacy: real responses contain real people's answers — names, emails, free text — and those would flow into the model's context. So I redact email addresses and aggregate rather than dumping raw answers, and I'd never send raw customer responses to a third-party model in production without that. Second, the account I'd demo against is a throwaway with no real responses, so there's no real personal data at stake and the privacy concern is a talking point rather than a live risk. The honest framing is: I know where the data goes, and I designed the seam so the demo stays simple while the real path stays one token away.
